netf-01.label: A team building a live video-conferencing app picks a transport protocol that accepts occasional dropped frames rather than pay the latency cost of retransmission and acknowledgment.
netf-01.sub: Which zone does this design choice belong to?
netf-01.why: Choosing UDP's best-effort delivery over TCP's reliability is a transport-layer design tradeoff, not an attack — nothing here overwhelms the service or forges an identity, which is what would move it to Common network attacks.

netf-02.label: A host on a LAN segment needs the MAC address behind a known IP address before it can build the next frame, so it broadcasts a request and caches the reply it gets back.
netf-02.sub: Which zone does this belong to?
netf-02.why: This is ARP doing its ordinary job of resolving a Layer 3 address to a Layer 2 address. The tempting neighbour is Common network attacks — ARP poisoning uses the same broadcast mechanism, but only when a third party forges replies to hijack the cache, which isn't happening here.

netf-03.label: A packet capture shows a client and server complete a three-step SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK exchange before a large file transfer begins, with every subsequent segment acknowledged in order.
netf-03.sub: Which zone does this belong to?
netf-03.why: A completed handshake followed by ordered, acknowledged delivery is TCP working exactly as specified. Contrast this with a flood of SYNs that never completes the handshake — that resource-exhaustion pattern is a DDoS technique that belongs to Common network attacks.

netf-04.label: A monitoring tool measures round-trip time to a remote host by sending an echo request and timing the echo reply that comes back.
netf-04.sub: Which zone does this belong to?
netf-04.why: This is ICMP performing its standard diagnostic function (ping). The tempting neighbour is Common network attacks, where the same echo-reply mechanism is weaponized against a spoofed victim's address at scale — that pattern, not a single diagnostic ping, is what earns the attacks zone.

netf-05.label: A network architect reviewing a live voice call's traffic notes a four-field, 64-bit datagram header carrying source port, destination port, length, and checksum — with no sequence number and no acknowledgment field anywhere in sight.
netf-05.sub: Which zone does this belong to?
netf-05.why: The absence of sequencing and acknowledgment fields is exactly what marks a UDP datagram header, distinguishing it from TCP's connection-oriented header — a protocol-identification exercise, not an attack scenario.

netf-06.label: A retailer places its public-facing web server and mail relay in a network zone reachable from the internet and sandwiched between two firewalls, while the internal accounting database sits entirely behind the inner firewall.
netf-06.sub: Which zone does this architecture belong to?
netf-06.why: Two firewalls bracketing internet-facing hosts is the defining shape of a DMZ (screened subnet). The tempting neighbour is a VLAN, but VLANs split a switch's broadcast domain for internal traffic — they don't define what the public internet is allowed to reach.

netf-07.label: A hospital wires billing terminals and clinical imaging workstations into the same physical switches on the same floor, but assigns them to separate broadcast domains that require a routing function for the two to exchange traffic.
netf-07.sub: Which zone does this architecture belong to?
netf-07.why: Splitting one physical switch fabric into separate broadcast domains is a VLAN's job. The tempting neighbour is microsegmentation, but that would isolate individual devices with per-workload policy — here whole departments share a segment, which is VLAN-scale granularity.

netf-08.label: A zero-trust program wraps a firewall rule around every individual database server in a cluster, so two servers hosting the same application still cannot reach each other unless a policy explicitly permits it.
netf-08.sub: Which zone does this architecture belong to?
netf-08.why: Isolation enforced down to a single server, even between peers running the same workload, is microsegmentation's signature. A VLAN would group that whole cluster into one shared broadcast domain rather than fencing off each server individually.

netf-09.label: A cloud team needs isolated network segments numbering far beyond a switch's 4,096-VLAN ceiling, so it tunnels Layer 2 traffic inside Layer 3 packets to stretch segmentation across subnets and data centers.
netf-09.sub: Which zone does this architecture belong to?
netf-09.why: Encapsulating Layer 2 segments over Layer 3 to exceed VLAN's numeric limit is the overlay technique that implements microsegmentation at cloud scale — the driving requirement (scale, per-workload flexibility) is what pushes this past a plain VLAN answer.

netf-10.label: An e-commerce company hosts its externally reachable order-API gateway in a zone bounded by two firewalls, with strict rules limiting what that zone may initiate toward the internal network even if the gateway itself is fully compromised.
netf-10.sub: Which zone does this architecture belong to?
netf-10.why: Bounding an internet-facing service between two firewalls and constraining its outbound reach is a DMZ's defense-in-depth pattern. Microsegmentation is the tempting neighbour, but that construct governs internal workload-to-workload traffic, not the internet-facing perimeter itself.

netf-11.label: A decade-old router still authenticates and encrypts using one static, shared RC4-based key for every device, and transmits its initialization vector in the clear alongside every packet.
netf-11.sub: Which zone does this configuration belong to?
netf-11.why: A static shared key and a cleartext IV describe WEP's cryptographic design, however broken. This is a protocol-generation identification, not an attack in progress — no one here is actively decrypting traffic or forging frames, which is what would move it to Common network attacks.

netf-12.label: A small office's new router requires every device to enter the same AES-based passphrase before joining, with no dedicated authentication server anywhere on the network.
netf-12.sub: Which zone does this configuration belong to?
netf-12.why: A shared passphrase without an authentication server is WPA2/WPA3-Personal mode, appropriate for a small deployment. This is the protocol operating exactly as intended for its use case, not a weakness being exploited.

netf-13.label: An enterprise requires every laptop to present a digital certificate to a dedicated authentication server, using port-based access control, before it is granted wireless access.
netf-13.sub: Which zone does this configuration belong to?
netf-13.why: Certificate-based authentication against a dedicated server through port-based access control is 802.1X/EAP enterprise mode — the design that scales wireless auth beyond a single shared secret.

netf-14.label: A campus network authenticates client devices using a zero-knowledge proof derived from Diffie-Hellman, relying only on a preset passphrase plus the hardware addresses of the handset and its access point.
netf-14.sub: Which zone does this configuration belong to?
netf-14.why: A zero-knowledge Diffie-Hellman derivative bound to a preset passphrase is WPA3's SAE (Dragonfly) exchange, an improvement over WPA2's PSK mode without requiring enterprise infrastructure — a generational upgrade, not an exploit.

netf-15.label: A security review flags that a still-deployed access point negotiates an encryption protocol that was built to replace WEP but has itself since been deprecated in favor of AES-CCMP.
netf-15.sub: Which zone does this finding belong to?
netf-15.why: Identifying that an AP still runs TKIP rather than AES-CCMP is placing a device on the wireless-generation timeline. Flagging a stale configuration is a design/lifecycle observation, distinct from an attacker actively exploiting that weakness in real time.

netf-16.label: An attacker floods a network's broadcast address with echo requests carrying a forged source address belonging to the intended victim, so every host on the segment replies to the victim at once.
netf-16.sub: Which zone does this scene belong to?
netf-16.why: Forging a source address to turn an entire broadcast segment into an amplification army is a smurf-style DDoS. The tempting neighbour is TCP/UDP & core protocols, since ICMP itself is legitimate — but weaponizing it at scale against a spoofed target is what moves this to the attacks zone.

netf-17.label: A rogue insider on the same LAN segment sends unsolicited replies associating their own MAC address with the default gateway's IP, so all outbound traffic quietly routes through their laptop first.
netf-17.sub: Which zone does this scene belong to?
netf-17.why: Forging address-resolution replies to hijack the gateway role is ARP spoofing enabling an on-path (MITM) position — the tempting neighbour is TCP/UDP & core protocols, since ARP itself is ordinary, but here it is actively falsified to redirect traffic.

netf-18.label: A traveler joins what looks like a hotel's official wireless network, unaware that an attacker nearby is broadcasting an identical network name to capture login credentials as they pass through.
netf-18.sub: Which zone does this scene belong to?
netf-18.why: A duplicated SSID luring victims onto an attacker-controlled access point is an evil-twin, on-path attack. The tempting neighbour is Wireless security generations, but this scene is about an attacker actively impersonating infrastructure, not a protocol's authentication design.

netf-19.label: A customer's browser is silently redirected to a fraudulent banking site after an attacker corrupts a resolver's cache with a forged record mapping the real bank's domain name to the attacker's own IP address.
netf-19.sub: Which zone does this scene belong to?
netf-19.why: Falsifying a cached DNS record to redirect a legitimate domain name is DNS (cache) poisoning — a live corruption of trusted resolution data, not DNS performing its ordinary lookup function.

netf-20.label: An attacker sends a continuous flood of connection-initiation packets carrying spoofed, unreachable source addresses, exhausting a web server's connection table before any legitimate handshake can complete.
netf-20.sub: Which zone does this scene belong to?
netf-20.why: A SYN flood with spoofed, unreachable sources is a deliberate resource-exhaustion DDoS technique. Contrast this with a normal completed three-way handshake, which belongs to TCP/UDP & core protocols — the difference is a flood of half-open connections that never legitimately complete.

network-foundations.hint: First ask: is this a protocol or architecture behaving as designed, or is someone actively attacking it right now? Only after that, sort by which construct or generation is at stake.
network-foundations.note: Wireless generations (WEP through WPA3) and segmentation constructs (VLAN, DMZ, microsegmentation) are grouped as single zones each — the discrimination inside those families is a finer-grained skill than this board tests. This board's job is the coarser sort: protocol design vs. segmentation architecture vs. wireless generation vs. active attack.
network-foundations.zones[0].def: The behavior and design tradeoffs of the transport-layer protocols and the core Layer 2/3 protocols that support them — TCP's connection-oriented, acknowledged, ordered delivery versus UDP's connectionless best-effort speed, plus utility protocols like ARP and ICMP doing their ordinary job. Sort a scene here when it describes how a protocol is built or chosen to behave, not when someone is abusing that same protocol to cause harm — that belongs to Common network attacks.
network-foundations.zones[1].def: The internal and perimeter architectures that keep traffic apart: VLANs splitting a switch's broadcast domain, a DMZ (screened subnet) sandwiching internet-facing hosts between two firewalls, and microsegmentation isolating traffic down to the individual workload under a zero-trust policy. The discrimination is granularity and purpose — VLAN groups many hosts by switch port, DMZ controls what the internet can reach, microsegmentation locks down even server-to-server traffic inside the trusted zone.
network-foundations.zones[2].def: The evolution of Wi-Fi authentication and encryption, from WEP's broken static RC4 key through WPA/WPA2's shared-passphrase or 802.1X/EAP enterprise modes to WPA3's AES-CCMP and SAE/Dragonfly key exchange. Sort a scene here when it describes what a protocol generation does or requires by design, not when an attacker is actively exploiting a wireless weakness in real time — that belongs to Common network attacks.
network-foundations.zones[3].def: Active exploitation of network protocols and trust relationships to intercept, disrupt, or redirect traffic — spoofing a trusted identity (ARP, IP, or an SSID), sitting on-path between two parties, overwhelming a target with volume, or corrupting a DNS answer. The discrimination rule is that someone is actively attacking right now, not that a protocol is merely behaving, or failing to behave securely, by design.
